passage: On his second day as an intern at the Bengaluru design studio, Ujjwal showed a logo draft to Joseph, the senior designer. Joseph's eyebrows shot up to his hairline. "Hmm. The orange. Interesting." Up again. Then down, then one up and one down. Ujjwal's stomach dropped. Was that disgust? Shock? Was he being mocked? He spent lunch redrawing the whole thing in grey. At four, Ritika from accounts passed his desk and saw the pile of discarded sketches. "Joseph?" she guessed. "Watch him order tea. His eyebrows do that for chai. His whole family talks like that; I met them at his wedding. Compare him with Joseph, not with you." Ujjwal watched. When the tea boy arrived, Joseph's eyebrows leapt exactly as high: "Ginger? Wonderful!" Ujjwal laughed out loud, walked over and asked him directly. "Oh, I liked the orange," Joseph said, brows dancing. "Keep it."

qa.q: What colour did Ujjwal redraw the logo in?
qa.a: Ujjwal redrew the whole thing in grey.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Joseph's eyebrows shot up?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt anxious and deflated, reading the eyebrows as disgust or mockery, when they were really Joseph's normal lively way of talking.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal read Joseph more accurately?
qa.a: Comparing Joseph's eyebrows with Joseph's own baseline, like when ordering tea, and then asking directly about the orange.

qa.q: How did Ritika see Joseph's eyebrows?
qa.a: Ritika knew them as Joseph's everyday style, even for chai, so she didn't read anything dramatic into them.

grounding: It shows one person's big eyebrow movements being read as dramatic by a newcomer, and learning to compare against that person's own normal.

subtype: Prolonged eye closure in exhaustion or calm [Mismatch]
passage:
Hi Vidya,
I owe you an apology for this morning's project meeting. When you sat with your eyes closed for most of my budget update, I said, in front of everyone, "Are we keeping you up?" A couple of people laughed. You opened your eyes, said "I'm listening", and repeated my three numbers back exactly. I felt about two inches tall. Afterwards Priyank told me you had come straight from a night shift at the hospital canteen, and also that you always close your eyes when you concentrate on numbers. I don't know which it was today, maybe both, and I should have asked instead of guessing. If you're stretched this week, we can move your part of the slides to Monday. Either way, I'm sorry for making a joke of it in front of the team.
Bhupen

qa.q: What did Bhupen say in front of everyone?
qa.a: Bhupen said, "Are we keeping you up?"

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling after Vidya repeated the numbers?
qa.a: Bhupen felt embarrassed and guilty, 'about two inches tall', realising the closed eyes had not meant boredom.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have done instead of joking?
qa.a: A gentle private check-in, asking whether Vidya was okay or needed a break, since closed eyes can mean tiredness, concentration or overwhelm.

qa.q: What was the meeting like for Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya, perhaps exhausted from a night shift or concentrating hard, was mocked in front of the team, yet stayed composed and proved to be listening.

grounding: It shows long eye closure in a meeting having several possible meanings, and a young adult regretting guessing instead of gently checking in.

subtype: Direct gaze in interviews and dating [Regulating]
passage: Pankaj had spent a month training for job interviews: firm handshake, steady eye contact, no looking at the floor. It worked; he got the offer. So on Saturday, meeting Aparna for coffee after their families had exchanged numbers, he did the same. The café near the station was deafening, a blender roaring every two minutes, and Aparna had exactly half an hour before her train. Pankaj leaned in and held her gaze, unblinking, while she talked about her botany course. Aparna's sentences got shorter. She kept looking at the sugar packets. "Is something wrong?" she finally asked. "You're looking at me like an exam invigilator." Pankaj laughed, embarrassed, and let his eyes drift to the window and back. "Sorry. Interview habits." Aparna relaxed. "I'm the opposite. I look everywhere except faces, especially when I'm nervous. But I'm listening, promise. You said your sister also studies botany?" She had heard every word.

qa.q: How long did Aparna have before her train?
qa.a: Aparna had exactly half an hour before her train.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when Aparna mentioned an exam invigilator?
qa.a: Pankaj felt embarrassed, laughing awkwardly, realising the interview habit didn't fit a coffee date.

qa.q: How did Pankaj adjust, and why did it help?
qa.a: He let his gaze drift to the window and back, softening it for a date instead of an interview, which let Aparna relax.

qa.q: What was the stare like for Aparna?
qa.a: Aparna felt uncomfortable, her sentences shrinking and eyes on the sugar packets; she finds eye contact hard herself but was still listening closely.

grounding: It shows a young adult shifting from steady interview eye contact to a softer gaze on a date, and a shy person listening well without much eye contact.

passage:
Monday. The hostel floor rep, Preeti, had a noise complaint to sort out: someone had played loud music on Sunday night. She asked Lalremsiami, "Were you in your room around eleven?" Lalremsiami looked up at the ceiling, then off to the side, lips moving slightly. "Sunday... I came back from church, then laundry... then, yes, room." Preeti noted the looking away and felt a small click of suspicion. People look away when they lie, don't they?
Wednesday. Before writing anything up, Preeti checked the facts. The gate register showed Lalremsiami signed in at 8:10. The warden's round sheet had her door marked "quiet, lights off" at 10:45. The music had come from the other wing.
Friday. At dinner someone asked Preeti what she had eaten on Tuesday. Preeti found herself staring at the ceiling fan, eyes flicking sideways, trying to remember. She laughed at herself. That weekend she told Lalremsiami, "Sorry I doubted you. You were just thinking."

qa.q: What time did the gate register show Lalremsiami signing in?
qa.a: The gate register showed she signed in at 8:10.

qa.q: What did Preeti feel when Lalremsiami looked up at the ceiling?
qa.a: Preeti felt a small click of suspicion, believing people look away when they lie; that was unfair, since Lalremsiami was only recalling the day.

qa.q: What did Preeti do right before writing anything up?
qa.a: Preeti checked the facts, the gate register and the warden's round sheet, instead of judging honesty from where someone looked.

qa.q: What was being questioned like for Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was simply trying to remember the day, eyes drifting up while listing church and laundry, and was answering honestly.

grounding: It shows looking up and away while recalling being mistaken for evasion, and checking the facts showing that gaze is no evidence of lying.

passage: In my first month as a trainee at the dental clinic, everyone wore masks all day, and I realised how much I had been reading mouths my whole life. When I explained a bill to a man at the front desk, I couldn't tell if he was smiling politely or gritting his teeth. His eyes crinkled, but that could have been squinting at the screen. I kept over-explaining, just in case. Payal, the senior assistant, pulled me aside at lunch. "Bidisha, behind a mask your voice has to do what your smile used to. And their eyes and words are all you get, so listen to those. If you can't tell, ask." The next patient was a nervous girl with her mother. Her eyes were wide above the mask and her hands gripped the chair. I said warmly, "First time here? You can squeeze the armrest as hard as you like." She nodded. I asked, "Scared, or just cold? It's freezing in here." She laughed. "Both."

qa.q: What did Payal say the voice has to do behind a mask?
qa.a: The voice has to do what the smile used to.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling while explaining the bill?
qa.a: Bidisha felt unsure and a bit anxious, unable to tell whether the man was smiling or gritting his teeth, which led to over-explaining.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do differently with the next patient?
qa.a: Bidisha used a warm voice, read the girl's wide eyes and gripping hands, and asked directly whether she was scared or cold.

qa.q: What might the nervous girl have felt when asked 'Scared, or just cold?'
qa.a: The girl likely felt understood and a little lighter, laughing and admitting 'Both'.

grounding: It shows masks hiding smiles and lower-face signals, so a young adult relies on voice, eyes and words and asks directly.

subtype: Nostril flare and tension in conflict [Interpreting]
passage:
"You said you'd do the dishes on Tuesdays," Jatin said. "It's Thursday. The pan has grown a personality."
"I've had lab till eight every day this week."
"So have I, and I still—"
Jatin stopped. Wasim's nostrils were flared wide, his cheeks tight, jaw working.
"Okay. Pause," Jatin said. "You look really angry. Are you? Or is it something else?"
"I just walked up six floors because the lift's broken again, and this flat is an oven." Wasim dropped his bag. "I'm boiling. Also, fine, a bit angry."
"At me?"
"At the pan. At the week. A little at you, for the personality line."
"Fair. That was a bit much."
"Give me ten minutes under the fan. Then we make a proper chore chart, because clearly our memory isn't working."
"Ten minutes. I'll get you water."
Later, cooler, Wasim scrubbed the pan himself while Jatin dried.

qa.q: How many floors did Wasim walk up?
qa.a: Wasim walked up six floors because the lift was broken again.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he noticed Wasim's flared nostrils?
qa.a: Jatin sensed the argument heating up and was worried Wasim was really angry, which made him stop mid-sentence; the signs turned out to be partly heat and effort.

qa.q: Why was Jatin's pause a good move?
qa.a: Stopping to ask 'Are you angry, or is it something else?' cooled things, brought out the stairs and the heat, and led to a practical chore chart.

qa.q: What was the argument like for Wasim?
qa.a: Wasim was hot and worn out from lab and six floors of stairs, a little angry at the week and the teasing line, and needed ten minutes to cool down.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading flared nostrils and tight cheeks as anger in a heated discussion when they also reflect effort and heat, and a pause and calm check-in helping.

passage:
"Gopika, sit down. The letter from the university came."
"Just read it, Harish."
"'We are pleased to offer you the full merit scholarship for the MSc in Marine Biology...'"
Gopika's jaw dropped. She didn't make a sound, just stood there, mouth wide open, one hand frozen halfway to her hair.
"Gopika? Say something. Are you okay?"
"...Full?"
"Full. Fees and hostel."
Then her face broke into the biggest grin he had ever seen, and she grabbed the letter and did a ridiculous dance round the dining table.
"Wait, wait," Harish said, reading on. "The course starts on the fifteenth of July. That's Achan's sixtieth birthday week."
Her jaw dropped again. Same open mouth. But this time her eyes filled, and she sat down slowly.
"I'll miss it," she said quietly. "His sixtieth."
Harish put a hand on her shoulder. "We'll celebrate early. July first. He'd want you to go."

qa.q: When does the course start?
qa.a: The course starts on the fifteenth of July.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after the jaw dropped the first time?
qa.a: Gopika was astonished, then overjoyed, breaking into a huge grin and dancing; the second jaw drop came with sadness at missing Achan's sixtieth.

qa.q: How did Harish respond to the second shock?
qa.a: He put a hand on her shoulder and offered a practical fix, celebrating early on July first, showing he understood it was upsetting.

qa.q: What was it like for Harish to see the first jaw drop?
qa.a: Harish couldn't tell if she was okay and asked her to say something, until the grin showed it was happy shock.

grounding: It shows a young adult's jaw dropping twice at surprising news, with the reaction that follows showing once joy and once sadness.
